                                                               3. Methods
2. Releated Works
                                                               3.1. Preliminaries: VLA models.
Vision-Language-Action Models. Vision-Language-Action
(VLA) models[5, 7, 9, 16, 24, 38, 42, 43, 52, 53] bridge       We use OpenVLA[24] as our backbone model. OpenVLA’s
visual-language understanding with robot control by map-       origin formulation is to adopt a discrete tokenization strategy
ping multimodal inputs to action outputs. Based on vision-     for robot action prediction through fine-tuning the Prismatic-
language models (VLM) [3, 8, 9, 13], VLAs represent robot      7B VLM backbone. The method frames action prediction as
actions (e.g., 6DoF motion, gripper control) as discrete to-   a vision-language task, mapping input observation images
kens compatible with text-based output. For example, RT-       and natural language instructions to discrete robot action
1[5] and RT-2[6] showed that dividing continuous actions       sequences. Specifically, continuous robot actions are dis-
into discrete bins allows integration with VLMs, enabling      cretized into 256 bins per dimension, with bin boundaries
zero-shot generalization using web-scale pretraining. Recent   determined by the 1st and 99th percentiles of training data
works[24, 32] further leverage this approach, demonstrating    distributions rather than min-max ranges to mitigate outlier
improved task generalization through large VLM backbones.      effects. This discretization converts N-dimensional actions
Building on this foundation, recent works have explored        into N discrete integers (0-255). To embed these into the
various approaches to improve VLA, such as leveraging          LLM’s vocabulary, OpenVLA overwrites the 256 least-used
3D visual inputs [53], integrating chain-of-thought reason-    tokens in the Llama tokenizer (last 256 tokens) rather than
ing [47], and employing parallel decoding strategies [25].     using special tokens, as the original tokenizer only reserves
In our work, we aim to simultaneously improve the perfor-      100 special tokens.
mance and execution speed of VLA.
                                                               3.2. Action Tokenizer via Residual VQ-VAE
Action Representation. Action representation is one of the
core components in robot policy learning. Classic action       Based on Residual VQ-VAE [4, 26, 48], we design our
representation schemes include high-level sub-tasks [2, 13],   encoder and decoder inspired by VAE in pyramidal flow
action primitives [20, 40], keypoints [12, 18], as well as     matching [23]. Instead of the simple Multi-Layer Perceptron
low-level continuous end-effector pose [27, 32] or joint       (MLP) used in Residual VQ-VAE [26, 48], we integrate 2D

Figure 1. The VQ-VLA pipeline, consisting of two main stages: (1) training a general convolutional residual VQ-VAE and (2) fine-tuning
OpenVLA using the LoRA approach. Specifically, a general convolutional residual VQ-VAE is first trained on the Open X-Embodiment
dataset, LIEBRO, and ManiSkill datasets. The trained VQ-VAE is then frozen and serves as an action tokenizer for OpenVLA, replacing the
simple binning method. In the second stage, OpenVLA is fine-tuned using the LoRA technique to optimize its performance.

                                                                                         4.2.3. Performance on Long-Horizon Tasks
                                                                                         VQ-VLA demonstrates outstanding performance on long-
                                                                                         horizon tasks (”Put all cups in the basket” and ”Put the
                                                                                         toy into the drawer”), significantly outperforming baseline
                                                                                         model in both success rate and efficiency. In scenarios where
Put all cups into the basket Put the toy into the drawer     Filp the pot upright        baseline models achieve success rates as low as 15% or
                                                                                         nearly 0, the VQO+L+M model achieves significantly higher
                                                                                         success rates of 50% and 30%, respectively (see Fig.3). For
                                                                                         the ”Put the toy into the drawer” task, a representative long-
                                                                                         horizon scenario, the baseline model was only able to com-
                                                                                         plete the first step of opening the drawer in 15 out of 20
                                                                                         trials, failing to proceed further in most cases. In contrast,
                                                                                         the VQO+L+M model successfully opened the drawer in
                                                                                         all test cases, demonstrating its robustness and reliability in
                                                                                         handling complex sequential tasks.

  VQO+L+M , achieves a success rate that is 23.25% higher than the Baseline on both short-horizon and long-horizon tasks. Additionally, the
  results show that VQO+L+M outperforms VQO+L , which in turn outperforms VQO , indicating the effectiveness of incorporating synthetic data
  during training without compromising real-world performance.
